chunks.text: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation Kamillo Ferry 1 , Anthea Monod 1 , and Keisuke Yano 2 1 Department of Mathematics, Imperial College London, UK 2 Institute of Statistical Mathematics, Japan † \dagger Corresponding e-mail: k.ferry@imperial.ac.uk

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) is now widely accepted as the standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its parameter efficiency arises from a low-rank factorization that is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model where parameter dimension alone cannot describe learning complexity. Singular learning theory overcomes the unsuitability of parameter dimension for capturing learning complexity by instead studying the real log canonical threshold (RLCT)—a geometric quantity which controls the leading asymptotic behavior of Bayesian generalization and model evidence. We study the RLCT for LoRA and, in particular, how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network in which the adaptation is performed. Under a local linearization of the pretrained network, we show that LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback–Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance. This covariance is constructed from the input activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer and determines which low-rank perturbations of the pretrained model are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression. When its kernel meets these directions, however, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters arise and the singular geometry of the model changes. We characterize this geometry both locally, using a decomposition into observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally, using affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. In particular, the global learning complexity is not necessarily determined by the

tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally, using affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. In particular, the global learning complexity is not necessarily determined by the geometry at a ground-truth parameter; it turns out that singularities on a different rank stratum can dominate the asymptotic behavior. To support the numerical study of this geometry, we introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT that accounts for finite-sample variation across inverse temperatures. Numerical experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.
Low-rank adaptation; singular learning theory; real log canonical threshold; low-rank matrix factorization; determinantal varieties.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) has become the standard method for fine-tuning large neural networks due to its parameter efficiency. Instead of updating pre-trained weight matrix W pre ∈ ℝ m × d W_{\text{pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} directly, LoRA freezes W pre W_{\text{pre}} and learns the following low-rank perturbation: W = W pre + B ​ A , B ∈ ℝ m × r , A ∈ ℝ r × d . W=W_{\text{pre}}+BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\,A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}. When r ≪ min ⁡ { m , d } r\ll\min\{m,d\} , the number of trainable parameters reduces significantly, however, a fundamental problem of identifiability also arises, since many pairs of matrices A , B A,B are able to represent the same update B ​ A BA . Approaching the problem of non-identifiability from a geometric perspective is useful in the sense that model parameters representing the same distribution may form a smooth manifold of constant dimension, so then the redundant directions can be removed locally. LoRA, however, turns out to be a singular statistical model. It turns out that the geometry of the factorized parameterization of LoRA changes with the rank of B ​ A BA , which results in a stratified parameter space in which different rank strata meet along singular loci.

Singular learning theory (SLT, Watanabe (2009) ; Watanabe (2018) ) is a methodology adapted for such statistical models where complex local geometry affects the asymptotic learning behavior. In regular models, local asymptotic behavior is controlled by a nondegenerate quadratic approximation to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and model complexity is captured simply by parameter dimension. In singular models, this quadratic approximation breaks down because the set of parameters representing the same distribution may have positive dimension, intersect itself, or change dimension across different strata. The asymptotics are then controlled by the local geometry of the zero set of the KL divergence and not just by the number of identifiable parameters. SLT studies this geometry and measures it using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT), which replaces half the parameter dimension in the leading asymptotics of Bayesian generalization and marginal likelihood. Computing the RLCT is therefore fundamentally a geometric problem that is closely connected to the study of singular algebraic and analytic varieties.

LoRA falls within this setting of singular statistical models since its factorized parametrization has a rich singular structure. The learning complexity of LoRA thus cannot be characterized by its nominal parameter dimension r ⁡ ( m + d ) r(m+d) . In addition to the low-rank geometric characterization of LoRA, the adapter is learned inside a pretrained network and the surrounding network determines which perturbations of the adapted weight matrix are distinguishable from the data. The learning complexity of LoRA is thus made up of interactions between the intrinsic geometry of the low-rank parameterization and the statistical geometry inherited from the pretrained model. The goal of this paper is to characterize this interaction and determine how it controls the RLCT of LoRA.

We develop a SLT framework for LoRA that explicitly characterizes the interaction between the geometry of the low-rank factorization and of the pretrained network. Under local linearization, we identify a forward-backward covariance which is constructed from layer activations and backpropagated sensitivities, and determines which directions of the LoRA update are statistically observable. This leads to two qualitatively different regimes: Under suitable nondegeneracy, we recover the classical RLCT of reduced-rank regression. In the degenerate case, the learning problem leads to affine linear sections of determinantal varieties; the different rank strata of these varieties compete to determine the asymptotic learning complexity. We develop both the local and global theory of this interaction and show that the global RLCT need not be determined by the singularity at a ground-truth parameter. For numerical RLCT estimation, we further introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator that accounts for finite-sample variation of the effective learning coefficient across inverse temperatures. Numerical experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures support our theory and demonstrate a strong layer dependence for the forward-backward geometry in neural networks.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We close this introduction with an overview and discussion of related work. Section 2 overviews the necessary background from SLT and the geometry of low-rank matrix factorizations. Section 3 formulates the local linearization of LoRA as a low-rank trace-regression problem, introduces the forward-backward covariance, and establishes conditions under which the classical RLCT of reduced-rank regression may be recovered. Section 4 studies the local singular geometry when these conditions fail and characterizes the contribution of statistically observable tangent directions, and reduces the remaining complexity to a residual singularity. Section 5 develops the global theory, using the gauge symmetry of the LoRA factorization to reduce the RLCT problem to affine linear sections of determinantal varieties and to compare singularities across different rank strata. Section 6 reviews numerical approaches to RLCT estimation, introduces our curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator, and studies our theory empirically on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures; in particular, we validate the local linearization and investigate the geometry of the forward–backward covariance in practice. Finally, we close the paper with a discussion of our results for low-rank adaptation and present some open questions in Section 7 .

Our work lies at the intersection of theoretical analyses of low-rank adaptation and singular learning theory. We now review existing literature and theory on LoRA and the local-linearization perspective on fine-tuning, as well as related work on surgical fine-tuning and choice of layers to adapt. We then position our work within the literature on RLCTs of singular statistical models and recent applications of SLT to neural networks. Finally, since our empirical analysis requires numerical computation of the RLCT, we review existing approaches to RLCT estimation and their relation to the estimator introduced in this work.

Theoretical understanding of LoRA remains limited. Zeng and Lee (2024) characterized its expressive power, and the convergence of LoRA training has been analyzed by Dayi and Chen (2024) ; Kim et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025) . However, its generalization behavior from the SLT viewpoint has not been investigated.

The local linearization in Section 3 , a key assumption of our analysis, is the approximation underlying the neural tangent kernel (NTK) view ( Jacot et al., 2018 , cf.) . Malladi et al. (2023) empirically showed that the NTK view describes prompt-based fine-tuning of language models well. Under the NTK view, Jang et al. (2024) proved that LoRA training has no spurious local minima.

Fine-tuning only a subset of layers, which we focus on in this paper, is known as surgical fine-tuning ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Lodha et al., 2023 ; Ando Ogawa et al., 2026 , c.f.,) . How to choose which layers to adapt is still an open question; for instance, Lodha et al. (2023) rank layers by their Fisher information while Ando Ogawa et al. (2026) rank them by the similarity of internal representations. Our analysis of how the RLCT depends on the choice of adapted layers sheds light on this question from the SLT viewpoint.

The RLCT or its upper bound has been computed analytically for various singular models: mixture models ( Yamazaki and Watanabe, 2003 ) , reduced rank regression ( Aoyagi and Watanabe, 2005 ) , and its extension to deep linear networks ( Aoyagi, 2024 ) , nonnegative matrix factorization ( Hayashi and Watanabe, 2017 ) , linear networks with a concept bottleneck structure ( Hayashi and Sawada, 2025 ) , Gaussian latent tree models ( Drton et al., 2017 ) and factor models ( Drton et al., 2025 ) , and three-layer neural networks ( Watanabe, 2001 ; Aoyagi et al., 2005 ; Aoyagi and Nagata, 2012 ; Kurumadani, 2026 ) . Watanabe (2026) studied the distinction between the RLCT of each layer and that of the whole network, i.e., layer-wise versus joint learning. Beyond model-specific derivations, Sergeant-Perthuis et al. (2026) proposed an algorithm that computes the local RLCT exactly for any model with two parameters. Since LoRA parameterizes the weight update as a low-rank product, it is natural to expect its RLCT to coincide with that of reduced rank regression ( Aoyagi and Watanabe, 2005 ) . We show that this holds under non-degeneracy of the forward-backward covariance ( Section 3.3 ), and that the two differ in general, both theoretically ( Section 4 and Section 5 ) and empirically ( Section 6 ).

Beyond analytical derivations, the relevance of SLT to deep learning has been argued by Wei et al. (2022) , and the local learning coefficient (LLC)—an estimable local version of the RLCT—has been applied to large models ( Lau et al., 2025 ) and used to track the developmental stages of transformers during training ( Hoogland et al., 2025 ) . Closely related to our work, Wang et al. (2025) refined the LLC to subsets of weights, such as individual attention heads, to compare the complexity of different components. We analytically show that the RLCT of the LoRA parameters in the adapted layers depends on the frozen pretrained network through the forward-backward covariance, and hence cannot be determined by the adapted layers alone.

Since the RLCT is analytically available only for limited classes of models, it is often estimated from posterior samples at inverse temperatures around 1 / log ​ n 1/{\rm log}n , based on the asymptotic expansion of the tempered posterior mean of the loss ( Watanabe, 2013 ) . Single-temperature estimators use the posterior at β ⋆ = 1 / log ​ n \beta^{\star}=1/{\rm log}n only: the WBIC-type estimators measure the gap between the posterior mean of the loss and either its value at a local minimizer ( Lau et al., 2025 ) or the empirical loss of the Bayes predictive distribution ( Takio and Suzuki, 2025 ) . The heat-capacity estimator ( Imai, 2019 ; Tokuda et al., 2022 ) uses the posterior variance of the loss. Multi-temperature estimators instead exploit how the tempered posterior mean of the loss varies with the inverse temperature: Watanabe (2013) proposed a two-temperature estimator, and Wei et al. (2022) regressed the tempered posterior mean of the loss on β − 1 \beta^{-1} over a set of inverse temperatures. For finite n n , however, the tempered posterior mean of the loss need not be linear in β − 1 \beta^{-1} , especially for deep models, which makes these estimators sensitive to the choice of temperatures (cf. Takio and Suzuki, 2025 , for the two-temperature estimator) . Our curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator ( Section 6 ) mitigates this sensitivity by a local quadratic fit in β − 1 \beta^{-1} .

In this section, we briefly overview and summarize the tools from SLT used throughout the paper. We first recall the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) and the basic properties that allow us to study it locally and using analytic ideals. Our main technical tool is a local splitting principle: after suitable analytic changes of coordinates, the regular directions of a statistical model can be separated from the singular part. The regular directions contribute to the RLCT in the usual dimension-counting manner, while the remaining contribution is encoded by the singularity of a lower-dimensional residual model.

Let q ⁡ ( x ) q(x) denote the true data-generating distribution and p ⁡ ( x ∣ w ) p(x\mid w) , w ∈ Ω w\in\Omega denote a statistical model. A natural measure of how well the parameter w w represents the truth is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence K ⁡ ( w ) = ∫ q ⁡ ( x ) ​ log ​ q ⁡ ( x ) p ⁡ ( x ∣ w ) ​ 𝑑 x . K(w)=\int q(x){\rm log}\frac{q(x)}{p(x\mid w)}\,\mathrm{d}{x}. Since K ⁡ ( w ) ≥ 0 K(w)\geq 0 , its zero set { w ∈ Ω : K ⁡ ( w ) = 0 } \{w\in\Omega:K(w)=0\} consists of the parameters for which the model represents the true distribution. In a regular identifiable model, locally, this zero set is an isolated point and K K has a nondegenerate quadratic approximation around it. In a singular model, however, the zero set may have positive dimension or singularities; K K may also vanish at different rates in different directions. This local behavior of K K determines how probability mass accumulates around parameters representing the truth. In Bayesian learning, the marginal likelihood is obtained by integrating the likelihood over parameter space and as the sample size grows, its leading asymptotic contribution comes from neighborhoods where K ⁡ ( w ) K(w) is small. The RLCT measures the rate of this concentration. In regular models, this rate is given simply by half the parameter dimension; in singular models, it depends on the geometry of K K near its zero set. This behavior can be studied using the zeta function associated with K K . Let Ω ⊂ ℝ n \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact semianalytic set and let ψ : Ω → ℝ \psi\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R} be nearly analytic. For an analytic function K ≥ 0 K\geq 0 , K ≢ 0 K\not\equiv 0 , consider the zeta function

Here ψ \psi is nearly analytic, i.e., it is a product of a real-analytic function and a positive smooth function ( Lin, 2017 ) . Throughout our work, we assume that the original prior ψ \psi is real-analytic and strictly positive in a neighborhood of the zero set of K K . Then coordinate changes multiply ψ \psi by a Jacobian determinant which yields a nearly analytic function. The function ζ \zeta admits a meromorphic continuation to the whole complex plane. The poles of this continuation are positive rational numbers ( Atiyah, 1970 ) and encode the rate at which K K vanishes near its zero set; the smallest pole defines the RLCT.

The remaining directions contain the essentially singular part of the model. Our aim is to separate these two contributions: after suitable analytic changes of coordinates, the regular directions will contribute s / 2 s/2 to the RLCT, and then what remains to be analyzed will be the singularity of a lower-dimensional residual model. In order to achieve our aim and make this reduction precise, we will use the notion of contact equivalence . Contact equivalence allows for both an analytic change of coordinates in the parameter space as well as an invertible analytic change of generators of the defining ideal. Both operations preserve the local RLCT.

Geometrically, these operations change the local representation of the singularity without changing the singularity relevant to the RLCT.

This proves the claim. If s = 0 s=0 or χ ≡ 0 \chi\equiv 0 , one of the two groups of generators is empty and there is nothing to add. ∎

We now adapt the singular learning framework given in Section 2 to low-rank adaptation. The factorization B ​ A BA determines the singular geometry of the LoRA parametrization, but by itself, it does not determine the statistical geometry of the adapted model. This is because the update is applied to a pretrained network, so its effect on the model output also depends on the activations entering the adapted layer and on how perturbations at that layer propagate through the remainder of the network. In this section, we will study this interaction in detail. Under a local linearization of the pretrained network, we first formulate the learning problem for a single LoRA-adapted layer as a low-rank trace-regression model. Its KL divergence is controlled by a covariance operator constructed from the forward activations and backpropagated sensitivities of the network, which we will refer to as the forward–backward (FB) covariance . Its geometry determines which perturbations of the adapted weight matrix are statistically distinguishable and therefore provides an interface between the low-rank geometry of LoRA and the statistical geometry derived from the pretrained model. We also identify a nondegenerate regime in which the FB covariance preserves all low-rank directions relevant to the adaptation problem. In this case, the KL divergence is equivalent to the Frobenius-norm loss of reduced-rank regression which recovers the classical RLCT. The failure of this nondegeneracy condition and the additional singular geometry that results will be further studied in Section 4 and Section 5 .

chunks.text: Positive definiteness as assumed in Proposition 3.1.3 is a much stronger assumption than necessary. Since S = B ​ A − B 0 ​ A 0 S=BA-B_{0}A_{0} has rank at most r + ρ r+\rho , the KL divergence only probes C C along a restricted family of low-rank directions. This motivates a weaker nondegeneracy condition adapted to the geometry of LoRA. From the eigendecomposition C = U ​ Λ ​ U ⊤ C=U\Lambda U^{\top} with a diagonal matrix Λ ∈ ℝ D × D \Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} and an orthogonal matrix U ∈ ℝ D × D U\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} , we get K ⁡ ( A , B ) = 1 2 ​ ‖ Λ 1 2 ​ U ⊤ ​ vec ⁡ ( S ) ‖ 2 . K(A,B)=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\Lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}U^{\top}\operatorname{vec}(S)\right\rVert^{2}. (2) Let V + ≔ im ⁡ C V_{+}\coloneqq\image C be the active subspace , so that ℝ D = V + ⊕ ker ⁡ C \mathbb{R}^{D}=V_{+}\oplus\ker C is an orthogonal decomposition. The orthogonal projection onto V + V_{+} is Π + ≔ U + ​ U + ⊤ \Pi_{+}\coloneqq U_{+}U_{+}^{\top} , where U + U_{+} consists of the columns of U U belonging to the positive eigenvalues. The covariance need not be positive definite on the ambient space: it is sufficient that its kernel contains no nonzero low-rank direction that can arise as a difference between admissible LoRA updates. In this case, projection onto the active subspace preserves the relevant low-rank geometry and the KL divergence remains equivalent to the reduced-rank regression loss and the classical RLCT of Aoyagi and Watanabe (2005) therefore captures the learning complexity. Outside of this regime, however, the kernel of the FB covariance intersects directions accessible to the low-rank model. Understanding the learning complexity in this case requires a more in-depth analysis of the geometry of the active coordinate map, which is the problem that will be studied in the following section.

We now study the local geometry of the model when the nondegeneracy condition of Section 3.3 fails. Recall that by Lemma 3.2.1 , the KL divergence is comparable to ‖ α ‖ 2 \left\lVert\alpha\right\rVert^{2} , where α ⁡ ( A , B ) = Π + ​ vec ⁡ ( B ​ A − B 0 ​ A 0 ) , \alpha(A,B)=\Pi_{+}\operatorname{vec}(BA-B_{0}A_{0}), and its zero set W Π W_{\Pi} consists of the parameters that are statistically indistinguishable from the ground truth under the locally linearized model. When ker ⁡ Π + \ker\Pi_{+} intersects the relevant low-rank directions, this zero set can contain additional geometry beyond the intrinsic non-identifiability generated by the LoRA factorization. Our aim in this section is to characterize this additional geometry locally around a point of W Π W_{\Pi} . The main idea is to separate directions that are already statistically observable to the first order from the remaining directions in which the active coordinate map is singular. The former component contributes a regular dimension-counting term to the RLCT, while the latter component determines a residual singularity. The contact-equivalence and splitting results of Section 2.2 provide the tools needed for us to make this decomposition rigorous.

We now study the singular geometry developed in the preceding sections numerically, which requires estimating the RLCT from finite-sample posterior computations. We first review existing single- and multi-temperature RLCT estimators and introduce a novel curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator designed to account for finite-sample variation of the effective learning coefficient across inverse temperatures. We then use these estimators to study the forward-backward covariance and learning complexity in three settings: synthetic trace regression with frozen neural-network features; transfer learning on rotated digits; and prompt-based surgical fine-tuning of a pretrained transformer.

(2025) . We use the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA, Roberts and Tweedie (1996) ) with a Gauss–Newton preconditioner computed at the initial point. We next consider a transfer task on the 8 × 8 8\times 8 handwritten digits of scikit-learn: a network pretrained on upright images is adapted to images rotated by 25 ∘ 25^{\circ} , with the digit value regressed as y = ( digit − 4.5 ) / 4.5 y=(\text{digit}-4.5)/4.5 . We refer to it as the rotated-digits task. LoRA is fitted on a small target set with 50 50 images per digit ( n = 500 n=500 ). We consider two architectures. • A four-hidden-layer ReLU MLP with widths ( 64 , 24 , 24 , 24 , 24 , 1 ) (64,24,24,24,24,1) : The adapted modules are fc1 : ℝ 64 → ℝ 24 \mathbb{R}^{64}\to\mathbb{R}^{24} , fc2 : ℝ 24 → ℝ 24 \mathbb{R}^{24}\to\mathbb{R}^{24} , fc3 : ℝ 24 → ℝ 24 \mathbb{R}^{24}\to\mathbb{R}^{24} , fc4 : ℝ 24 → ℝ 24 \mathbb{R}^{24}\to\mathbb{R}^{24} .

• A two-block transformer whose tokens are the 8 8 image rows: The input is embedded into dimension d model = 16 d_{\mathrm{model}}=16 , the number of heads is 2 2 , a feed-forward width is 32 32 , and a CLS readout is installed. The adapted modules are q_proj (query projection) and v_proj (value projection) and ffn_down (output projection of feed-forward network) in each block. LoRA of rank r = 8 r=8 is inserted into one module at a time, all other weights frozen, and fitted by Adam on the squared loss without weight decay. For the posterior computation, the likelihood is Gaussian with the noise variance set to the training mean squared error at the fitted point w ^ \hat{w} , and the localized prior 𝒩 ⁡ ( w ^ , γ − 1 ​ I ) \mathcal{N}(\hat{w},\gamma^{-1}I) uses γ = 1 \gamma=1 . The FB covariance spectra of the two architectures differ qualitatively (Figure 4 ). In the MLP, the spectrum of every module has an exact kernel: its spectrum drops to numerical zero well before the last index. In the transformer, the eigenvalues decay over many orders of magnitude, so the FB covariance C C seems to be effectively degenerate. Figure 5 shows all RLCT estimates per module, together with the quadratic prediction λ quad ​ ( β ⋆ ) \lambda_{\mathrm{quad}}(\beta^{\star}) of the Laplace approximation and the value 1 2 ​ r ​ ( m + d − r ) \frac{1}{2}r(m+d-r) of Aoyagi and Watanabe (2005) with the true rank equal to the LoRA rank. All estimates lie far below the latter, and most of them agree with λ quad ​ ( β ⋆ ) \lambda_{\mathrm{quad}}(\beta^{\star}) , except for fc1 and the first transformer block. They also depend on the layer: within the MLP they decrease from fc1 to fc4 , and the smallest value, for fc4 , goes with the largest kernel of the FB covariance.

Figure 6 studies the validity of local linearization in our study. We see that the relative linearization is small during the early phase of fine-tuning, which supports the use of FB features computed at the pretrained weights as a local description of the adaptation problem. As training progresses, we see that the error steadily increases and eventually reaches order 1, which indicates that higher-order effects become important as the adapted model moves away from pretrained initialization. The rate of this diversion depends on layer, since some layers appear to be still approximated well by the linearized model than others. Thus, our linearized theory should be taken as a characterization of the local singular geometry of LoRAa around the pretrained model, and not so much as an approximation of the full nonlinear fine-tuning trajectory.

Figure 7 showcases the FB covariance spectra for query and value units. The spectrum decays more slowly in shallower layers. The value units show a clear monotone ordering in depth, whereas the query units of layers 4–12 have nearly the same spectrum. Figure 8 showcases the RLCT estimates. All estimates lie below the half of rank of the Fisher information matrix that is bounded by N / 2 = 256 N/2=256 , and hence far below the Aoyagi and Watanabe (2005) value 1 2 ​ r ​ ( p + q − r ) = 6112 \frac{1}{2}r(p+q-r)=6112 for reduced rank regression. Also, the RLCT is not determined by the Laplace approximation alone. Finally, both the spectra and the RLCT depend strongly on the layer.

In this paper, we studied the learning complexity of LoRA from the perspective of singular learning theory. Our main conclusion is the complexity is determined by multiple factors and not only the low-rank parameterization by itself. It turns out to depend on how the geometry of the low-rank update interacts with the statistical geometry from the pretrained network. Under local linearization, the FB covariance interfaces between these two geometries and determines which perturbations of an adapted weight matrix are statistically observable. As a result, LoRA modules with the same rank and parameter count can have very different learning complexities depending on where they are located in a network. Our experimental results suggest that this dependence on the pretrained network is significant in practice. Both the spectrum of the FB covariance and the RLCT vary significantly across layers and modules. In particular, degeneracy of the covariance in the ambient weight space does not determine the learning complexity of LoRA alone: what matters is how the degeneracy interacts with the low-rank directions that the adapter sees and interacts with. More broadly, this distinction may be useful in studying parameter-efficient adaptation, where nominal parameter count by itself gives only a limited description of the effective complexity of the learning problem.

Our work suggests several possible directions for future research. One such direction is a further in-depth of the FB covariance itself, in the sense that its geometry may depend on model architecture, pretrained representation, data distribution, downstream task, and location of the adapted module. In our experiments, we observed strong layer dependence which suggests that the FB covariance could provide information or indicate where a model should be adapted. Selecting layers or modules for fine-tuning also remains an open problem; it would be interesting to study whether the FB geometry or the corresponding learning complexity can help predict which adaptation locations are the most effective and how this may relate to existing criteria for surgical fine-tuning. Importantly, our theoretical study considers only a single layer at a time. In practice, LoRA is often applied simultaneously to multiple layers or modules. Extending our framework to this multiple setting would entail a further study of the associated geometry of each adaptation location, as well as of how the statistically observable directions interact across the network. More broadly, this raises the question of how learning complexity distributes over components of the pretrained models and how they interact under parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Our work and proposed framework provides a starting point for such questions.
